extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature (scientists, students, and educated public)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative guidance about scientific education, physiological training, and experimental inference in animal behaviour and fossil-plant classification. Contains recommendations for students, institutions, and experimental methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal study of recommended textbooks
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must study at home the textbooks recommended by the lecturer in order to profit from lectures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lectures alone produce only transient impressions; active home work (e.g., doing problems rather than only listening) is necessary to acquire the attitude of mind by which facts were discovered and can be understood and used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire inductive and deductive habits of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Learners should develop the inductive habit (arranging and judging facts) and the deductive habit (using arranged facts practically).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These habits are formed by personal, continuous study of a subject; they cannot be gained by passive lecture-watching and are central to scientific understanding and application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth over superficial breadth of study
rubrics_metrics.description: Study one subject thoroughly rather than many superficially to learn how to learn and to gain transferable learning skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By learning how to learn one thing thoroughly, the student will be better prepared to learn other subjects in turn; scattered study yields poor mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat lectures as aids, not substitutes, for learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Good lectures are intended to teach students how to use their own eyes and minds, not to do the learning for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on lectures as the sole source of knowledge—use them as guides to direct active personal study and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional responsibility to teach practical health science
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions in manufacturing districts should expand instruction in physiology toward practical health to improve public wellbeing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given local needs and an audience accustomed to applying scientific laws, institutions can and should teach the physical science of health (e.g., classes focused on preserving health, sanitation, and applied physiology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Core personal-health measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals should apply known laws of personal health: healthy habitations, personal cleanliness, pure air, pure water, and unadulterated food.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These measures are already known and can be applied safely by any adult; improving these reduces disease and builds stronger bodies over generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sensory-deprivation and controlled-stimulus experiments to infer instinct
rubrics_metrics.description: To test whether a behaviour is innate, deprive subjects of particular senses (dark rearing, sealing ears, hoods) and then present controlled stimuli to observe responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: chickens hatched and kept in the dark that, when exposed to a hen's call for the first time, run straight to the hen indicate that sounds were not merely meaningless sensations; sealing ears and later presenting sound produced directed runs to the sound source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral criteria for identifying instinctive actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Instinctive behaviours are immediate, directed, species-typical actions observable without prior experience (e.g., precise pecking, running toward a brood-mother by sound alone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support for instinct includes rapid accuracy (striking within a hair’s-breadth), repeatability across individuals, and occurrence early in life (within minutes or days of hatching) without prior learning opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure of cross-species imitation as evidence for instinct
rubrics_metrics.description: If an individual exposed continuously to another species' behaviour does not adopt that behaviour, this supports that the behaviour is instinctive rather than acquired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a chicken raised alongside a turkey did not learn the turkey's fly-catching art despite constant exposure, suggesting species-specific instinctual limits on learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use controlled placement and environmental manipulation in behavioural tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Design experiments that manipulate location, distance, obstacles, and sensory access to test perception and behaviour (e.g., place subjects at set distances, on rough ground, inside boxes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations such as the animal's trajectory (straightness), ability to leap or avoid obstacles, number of strikes before capture, and reactions when senses are temporarily blocked provide diagnostic data on perception and instinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer reproductive/fruiting organs over vegetative characters for taxonomic classification
rubrics_metrics.description: In fossil-plant classification, conclusions based on vegetative organs (e.g., stems) must yield to evidence from organs of fructification (fronds, fruits) when available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although stem structure can be informative, classification should be revised if reproductive organs provide clearer affinities; do not create new higher taxa solely on vegetative characters when reproductive evidence aligns with existing groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlate fronds and stems by consistent association and morphological correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the co-occurrence of fronds with stems in specimens and correspondence of stipe-base sizes to leaf scars as the best available evidence for linking fronds to stems in fossils short of organic union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These correlations are the strongest inferential evidence in paleobotany when direct organic connection is absent, but remain tentative and should be treated with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group fossil stems by distinctive stem-structure characters and compare to living analogues
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish fossil-fern groups by key stem features (e.g., central medulla with continuous vascular cylinder and regular meshes vs parenchymatous axis with perpendicular vascular tracts) and compare these structures with living monocotyledonous or dicotyledonous analogues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent anatomical peculiarities of stems to establish groups, but interpret affinities by analogy to living forms while acknowledging unique permanent elements that may lack modern analogues.
